subject: geography
title: Cambridge IGCSE Geography (0460)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge IGCSE Geography 0460 syllabus for 2027, 2028 and 2029 (version 2)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topics 1 to 10, their numbered sub-sections (1.1, 1.2, ...) and the numbered content statements used as objective codes (1.1.1, ...) are transcribed from the syllabus. The 'Geographical skills' section is not numbered in the syllabus: its code S and sub-section codes S.1 to S.5 and their objective codes are ours. Objective statements are our own paraphrase.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-08): the official PDF (version 2, published October 2024) for examination in 2027, 2028 and 2029, read through a pdftotext rendering. In the rendering the content-statement numbers are sometimes misaligned with their text (for example in 1.1, 1.3, 2.1, 4.4, 5.1, 7.2, 8.1 and 9.1); the codes were matched to statements by order. Check the objective codes against the PDF.

Assessment overview as read: all candidates take Paper 1 Physical Geography (1 hour 45 minutes, 75 marks, 36%: Section A one compulsory 25-mark structured question; Section B two from three 25-mark structured questions; topics 1-5) and Paper 2 Human Geography (1 hour 45 minutes, 75 marks, 36%; same structure; topics 6-10), and either Component 3 Coursework (one fieldwork assignment of 1800-2200 words, 60 marks, 28%, internally assessed) or Paper 4 Geographical Investigations (1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks, 28%: two compulsory 30-mark questions on fieldwork methodology, hypotheses, data presentation, analysis and evaluation). Calculators may be used in all examinations. Grades A* to G; there are no Core/Extended tiers.

Changes in this version (from the syllabus): content split into physical (Paper 1) and human (Paper 2) topics; a new climate-change topic; the settlement, water and weather topics removed; the specific skills paper removed (skills are tested in all components); Paper 2 now matches Paper 1 (75 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes); Paper 4 renamed Geographical Investigations; MEDC/LEDC replaced by HIC/MIC/LIC; case studies replaced by 'detailed specific examples', which the syllabus does not name.

This version is examined from 2027. A student sitting the examination in 2026 is examined on the 2024-2026 syllabus, which is not in the repository; the 2027-2029 version is published as the current version because new students now will sit 2027 or later.
The platform cannot run the coursework component; lessons and practice cover its fieldwork skills, and the mocks simulate Papers 1, 2 and 4.

components.name: Paper 1: Physical Geography
components.description: Section A: one compulsory 25-mark structured question. Section B: two from three 25-mark structured questions. Short-answer and extended-response items, some based on source material; topics 1 to 5.

components.name: Paper 2: Human Geography
components.description: Section A: one compulsory 25-mark structured question. Section B: two from three 25-mark structured questions. Short-answer and extended-response items, some based on source material; topics 6 to 10.

components.name: Component 3: Coursework
components.description: Alternative to Paper 4: one teacher-set fieldwork assignment of 1800-2200 words, internally assessed and externally moderated.

components.name: Paper 4: Geographical Investigations
components.description: Alternative to Component 3: two compulsory 30-mark questions on fieldwork-based investigations (methods, hypotheses, data presentation, analysis, conclusions and evaluation).

children.name: The main hydrological characteristics and processes which operate in rivers and drainage basins

objectives.text: Describe the characteristics of rivers and drainage basins: long profile, width, depth, velocity, discharge, wetted perimeter, channel, watershed, tributary, confluence, source and mouth.
Use the Bradshaw model to describe how channel characteristics change downstream.
Explain how a drainage basin operates within the water cycle.
Describe the processes in a drainage basin, from precipitation and interception to throughflow, groundwater flow and evapotranspiration.
Explain river erosion, transportation and deposition processes.

children.name: The main landforms associated with these processes

objectives.text: Describe and explain the formation of waterfalls, rapids, gorges, V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs, potholes, meanders, oxbow lakes, levées, floodplains and deltas.

children.name: Rivers present opportunities and hazards for people

objectives.text: Describe the opportunities and hazards of living near a river.
Explain the human and natural causes of river flooding.
Describe the impacts of river flooding.
Evaluate strategies and techniques for managing river flooding, including sustainable ones.
Explain the human causes of river pollution.
Describe the impacts of river pollution.
Evaluate strategies and techniques for managing river pollution, including sustainable ones.
Detailed specific example: the causes, impacts and management of a flood on a named river.
Detailed specific example: the causes, impacts and management of pollution in a named river.

children.name: Physical processes that shape the coast

objectives.text: Explain coastal erosion, transportation, deposition and longshore drift.
Describe constructive and destructive waves and wave refraction.

children.name: The main landforms associated with these processes

objectives.text: Describe and explain the formation of headlands, bays, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, stumps, beaches, spits, bars and sand dunes.
Explain the formation and characteristics of concordant and discordant coastlines.

children.name: Coasts present opportunities and hazards for people

objectives.text: Describe the opportunities of living near the coast.
Describe the hazards of living near the coast.
Evaluate hard and soft engineering for managing coastal erosion and flooding, including sustainable approaches.
Describe the distribution and impacts of tropical storms (cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons).
Evaluate preparation, planning, protection and prediction for managing tropical storms.
Describe the distribution and importance of coral reefs and mangroves, the threats to them and how they are protected and managed.
Detailed specific example: coastal erosion and protection from tropical storms on a named coast.
Detailed specific example: the importance of, threats to and management of a named coral reef.

topics.name: Changing ecosystems
topics.description: Paper 1 (Physical Geography). The Antarctic content has no detailed specific example because it is based on Antarctica only.

objectives.text: Locate the Antarctic ecosystem.
Explain the characteristics of the Antarctic climate.
Describe the features of the Antarctic ecosystem.
Explain the links between abiotic and biotic factors in Antarctica and how plants and animals adapt.

children.name: Threats to the Antarctic ecosystem and how they can be managed

objectives.text: Describe threats to Antarctica such as resource exploitation, climate change, fishing and tourism.
Describe the impacts of damage to the Antarctic ecosystem.
Evaluate strategies for managing Antarctica, such as international agreements and environmental impact surveys.

children.name: Characteristics of the tropical rainforest ecosystem

objectives.text: Describe the global distribution of tropical rainforests.
Explain the characteristics of the equatorial climate.
Describe the characteristics and structure of the tropical rainforest.
Explain the links between abiotic and biotic factors in the rainforest and how plants and animals adapt.

children.name: Threats to tropical rainforest ecosystems and how they can be managed

objectives.text: Describe threats to tropical rainforests such as logging, farming, ranching, roads, HEP and settlement.
Describe the impacts of rainforest destruction and deforestation.
Evaluate strategies for managing tropical rainforests, including sustainable ones.
Detailed specific example: threats, impacts and management in a named rainforest area.

children.name: The structure of the Earth and distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes

objectives.text: Describe the layers of the Earth: inner core, outer core, mantle, crust and lithosphere.
Name and locate the main tectonic plates and explain how they move.
Describe the types of plate boundary and the location of earthquakes and volcanoes.

children.name: The processes and features associated with earthquakes and volcanoes

objectives.text: Explain the processes at each type of plate boundary that cause earthquakes and eruptions.
Describe the focus, epicentre and seismic waves of an earthquake.
Describe strato-volcanoes, shield volcanoes and cinder cones.
Classify volcanoes as active, dormant or extinct.
Describe the main features of a volcano.
Describe volcanic hazards and the significance of their speed, size, frequency and spread.
Explain why people live in areas at risk from earthquakes and eruptions.
Describe the impacts of earthquakes.
Describe the impacts of volcanic eruptions.
Describe how the magnitude of tectonic events is measured (moment magnitude, Richter and Mercalli scales; the volcanic explosivity index).

children.name: Managing the impacts of tectonic hazards

objectives.text: Distinguish primary and secondary responses.
Evaluate monitoring, prediction, protection, planning and technology for managing earthquakes and eruptions.
Detailed specific example: the causes, impacts, responses and management of a named earthquake.
Detailed specific example: the causes, impacts, responses and management of a named volcanic eruption.

topics.name: Climate change
topics.description: Paper 1 (Physical Geography). A new topic in this version.

children.name: The natural and human causes of climate change

objectives.text: Describe the evidence for climate change.
Explain natural factors in climate change: orbital changes, sunspots and volcanic activity.
Explain how human activity causes the enhanced greenhouse effect.

children.name: The impacts of climate change at a range of geographic scales

objectives.text: Describe present and predicted impacts of climate change such as sea-level rise and changes to temperature, weather and food production.
Describe strategies, including agreements, and techniques used to manage the impacts of climate change.
Evaluate mitigation and adaptation strategies and techniques.
Detailed specific example: the impacts of and responses to climate change in a named country or region.
Describe patterns and trends in global population growth.
Explain reasons for population growth and decline using fertility, birth and death rates, natural increase and migration.
Evaluate the impacts of pro-natalist and anti-natalist policies on birth rates.
Describe the demographic transition model and its strengths and limitations.
Explain how natural increase and net migration influence population structure.
Explain the causes of youthful and ageing populations and evaluate their impacts.
Detailed specific example: population change and a population policy in a named country.

children.name: The causes and impacts of international migration

objectives.text: Distinguish economic migrants, asylum seekers and refugees.
Explain the causes of migration, including push and pull factors.
Describe the impacts of migration on migrants and on origin and destination countries.
Evaluate strategies for managing international migration.
Detailed specific example: a named international migration, its causes, impacts and management.
Explain variations in urban growth rates around the world.
Explain the causes of rapid urban growth in LICs.
Describe the opportunities of urban living.
Describe the opportunities and challenges of rapid urban growth, including unplanned settlements.
Describe the impact of urban sprawl on the rural-urban fringe.
Evaluate strategies and techniques for managing urban growth, including sustainable ones.
Detailed specific example: the causes, challenges, opportunities and management of growth in a named urban area.
Describe social and economic indicators of development.
Use indicators to compare countries and evaluate their usefulness.
Explain the factors affecting quality of life and standard of living.
Explain the reasons for differences in development and the development gap.
Describe the current global pattern of LICs, MICs and HICs.
Define sustainable development.
Describe social, economic and environmental strategies for sustainable development.
Evaluate trade, aid and debt relief as ways of reducing uneven development.
Detailed specific example: the development and development strategies of a named LIC or MIC.
Classify industries as primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary.
Describe how employment structures change in LICs, MICs and HICs.
Explain the factors influencing the location and distribution of industries.

children.name: The impact of globalisation and the role of transnational corporations

objectives.text: Explain what is meant by globalisation.
Describe the key features of globalisation.
Describe the impacts of globalisation on trade, transport, culture, communications and technology.
Describe the role and global organisation of TNCs.
Evaluate the impacts of TNCs on host countries.
Detailed specific example: globalisation and a named TNC in a named country or area.
Explain the growth of tourism as an industry.
Describe the Butler model and its strengths and limitations.
Describe the benefits and problems of tourism at a range of scales.
Evaluate strategies for managing tourism sustainably.
Detailed specific example: the growth, impacts and management of tourism in a named country or area.
Describe farming types, including subsistence, commercial, arable, pastoral, mixed, aeroponics, aquaponics and hydroponics.
Describe farming systems as inputs, processes and outputs.

children.name: The global patterns of food supply and demand

objectives.text: Describe global patterns of calorie intake and explain the variations.
Explain changes in global food production and consumption.
Describe strategies used to increase food supply.
Explain the globalisation of food supplies.
Describe the impacts of the globalisation of food supplies.
Describe human and natural factors that reduce food supply.
Describe the problems of food insecurity in countries at different levels of development.
Describe strategies and techniques for increasing food supply.
Evaluate the role of food aid in improving food security.
Evaluate strategies for managing desertification and soil erosion, including sustainable ones.
Detailed specific example: food supply and food insecurity in a named country or area.
Classify energy types as renewable, non-renewable, or (fuelwood) either.

children.name: The global patterns of energy supply and demand

objectives.text: Explain the increasing global production and consumption of energy.
Describe global patterns of energy surplus and deficit and explain the importance of energy security.
Explain variations in energy use within and between countries at different levels of development.
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
Describe strategies and techniques for increasing energy supply.
Evaluate strategies for managing energy supplies, including sustainable ones.
Detailed specific example: the energy mix, impacts and energy management of a named country.

topics.name: Geographical skills
topics.description: Skills that apply across all components (not numbered in the syllabus). Includes the fieldwork skills and enquiry route tested in Component 3 and Paper 4.

objectives.text: Select, construct and interpret maps using direction, scale, symbols and a key.
Use coordinates, latitude and longitude, and four- and six-figure grid references.
Give directions with the 16-point compass and bearings from grid north; measure distances and areas.
Use gradient, contours and spot heights, calculate height differences and interpret cross-sections and transects.
Interpret atlas, choropleth, desire-line, flow-line, isoline, topographical and other thematic maps at 1:50 000 and 1:25 000.
Construct graphs, charts and diagrams with suitable scales and annotations.
Interpret and evaluate information on graphs, including climate graphs, population pyramids and flood hydrographs.
Identify variations, trends and patterns in data.
Interpret photographs (ground, oblique and vertical aerial), cartoons, diagrams and satellite images.
Analyse written sources and recognise bias.
Use GIS to identify trends and patterns and solve problems, and recognise its benefits and limitations.
Use number, area, scale, standard notation and significant figures.
Calculate and use mean, median, mode, range, percentages, ratios and proportions.
Describe relationships and trends, interpolate and extrapolate, and identify weaknesses in statistical presentations.

children.name: Fieldwork skills and the route to geographical enquiry

objectives.text: Follow the route to geographical enquiry from hypothesis to evaluation.
Select and use fieldwork equipment such as ranging poles, flow meters, quadrats, noise meters and clinometers.
Select, conduct or describe fieldwork techniques such as questionnaires, counts, surveys, transects and field sketches.
Devise data collection sheets and risk assessments.
